title: Crabka — Gres Query Traces
description: Distributed traces from crabka-gres, the PostgreSQL-compatible SQL engine. Every panel filters on span attributes rather than span names: the statement span sets otel.name, so it is exported under the query summary ("SELECT demo_orders"), never under a literal name like db.statement.

panels.title: Recent query traces
panels.description: One row per trace. Click a trace id to open the waterfall: gres.session → gres.statement → the engine's statement span → pg.select / pg.write → pg.timestamp.read, gres.wal_append, gres.exec_read; a write also has pg.commit.

panels.title: Statement spans
panels.description: Matched on db.system.name, NOT on a span name. The statement span records otel.name = its query summary, so it exports as "SELECT demo_orders" and a query for a span named db.statement returns nothing.

panels.title: Slow statements (> 50 ms)
panels.description: The starting point for "which step was slow" — open one and read the child durations.

panels.title: Failed statements
panels.description: Statement spans whose status is ERROR. error.type and db.response.status_code both carry the five-character SQLSTATE; otel.status_description carries the message.

panels.title: Executor reads
panels.description: gres.exec_read is the executor body under pg.select / pg.write. Widen crabka_pgexec::exec to =trace via CRABKA_OTLP_FILTER to also get the pg.blocking_worker and pg.scan spans underneath it.

panels.title: Commits
panels.description: pg.commit carries pg.gate_wait_ms — time spent waiting for the group-commit gate, the single most useful commit-latency field.

panels.title: WAL appends
panels.description: gres.wal_append is the durable write into the broker, with pg.wal.frames / bytes / first_offset / last_offset. It also injects a traceparent Kafka header, so a WAL apply on a follower or a later replay links back to this trace rather than parenting under it.

options.content:
**Filter on attributes, not span names.** `gres.statement` and `db.statement` set `otel.name` to the query summary, so they are exported as `SELECT demo_orders`. Use `span.db.system.name = "postgresql"` to select statement spans.

**Fixed span names** you can match directly: `gres.session`, `gres.parse`, `pg.select`, `pg.write`, `pg.commit`, `pg.scan`, `pg.blocking_worker`, `gres.exec_read`, `pg.route`, `pg.timestamp_scatter`, `pg.prewrite`, `pg.resolve`, `gres.wal_append`, `gres.wal_apply`, `kv.apply`, `wal.chunk`, `tso.grant`, `range.barrier`, and — on a multi-range cluster only — `gres.range_rpc` / `gres.range_serve`.

**Join your own trace.** Append a sqlcommenter comment to any query and gres adopts it as the parent:

```sql
SELECT count(*) FROM demo_orders /*traceparent='00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01'*/
```

OTel-instrumented Postgres drivers emit that automatically. The `gres-workload` container tags one statement per pass with a fresh random traceparent, so this dashboard always has an example.

**More detail on demand.** The default `CRABKA_OTLP_FILTER` enables the session, statement, executor, routing and WAL tiers at `DEBUG`. Set `CRABKA_OTLP_FILTER=info,crabka_pgexec::exec=trace` (plus the other tiers you want) on the `gres` service for per-scan and contended-row-lock spans.

**Verbatim SQL is off.** `db.query.text` appears only when `CRABKA_OTLP_SQL_TEXT=true`; it exports literals, so it is the one setting here that can leak secrets or personal data. `db.query.summary`, `db.operation.name` and `db.collection.name` are always present.
